To decide who forms the government and to control the government (e.g. by demanding answers from ministers).
What does it mean that Denmark is a parliamentary democracy?
That a government cannot be appointed if a majority in the Folketing is against it. The Folketing decides who holds governmental power.
What can happen if a government finds the majority against it on an important matter (e.g. the budget)?
The government can resign or call an election.
Does Denmark have an upper house that must approve the Folketing's decisions?
Are the Folketing's meetings open to ordinary citizens?
Yes, the meetings are normally public. You can also follow them on TV and on the Folketing's website.
When is question time in the Folketing?
Every Wednesday – ministers answer questions from members of the Folketing.
How many readings must a bill have in the Folketing?
Three readings before it can be passed.
What are the Folketing's committees?
Standing committees that roughly correspond to the ministries. They deal with bills between the three readings and put questions to the minister.
What do the Legal Affairs Committee and the European Affairs Committee work on?
Legal Affairs Committee: police, courts and punishment. European Affairs Committee: Denmark's relationship with the EU.
Can citizens and associations contact the Folketing's committees and members?
Yes. They can write, email or call and ask for a meeting. Citizens can also freely write to members of the Folketing.
What power does the government have besides being part of the legislative power?
The executive power – the government and the authorities implement and administer the laws through the ministries.
Who puts forward by far the most bills?
The government.
Who leads the government, and how many ministers are there normally?
The prime minister. Normally about 20 ministers.
Who decides who will be a minister, and how many there will be?
The prime minister alone.
Do ministers have to be members of the Folketing?
They usually are, but they do not have to be.
Who decides that ministries are merged or created?
The prime minister (usually after a general election).
Who is responsible for what goes on in a ministry?
The individual minister.
What is a coalition government?
A government in which several parties hold governmental power together.
What is the difference between a majority government and a minority government?
Majority government: the government parties together have a majority in the Folketing. Minority government: they do not have a majority and depend on support from other parties.
What are parties outside the government that support a minority government called?
Support parties (støttepartier).
What are government parties?
The political parties that have ministers in the government.
What type of government have most Danish governments since 1945 been?
Minority governments.
Which four parties make up the current government?
The Social Democrats, SF (Socialist People's Party), the Moderates and the Social Liberals (Radikale Venstre).
What is a representative democracy?
The people elect politicians to the Folketing, who take care of legislation on the people's behalf.
How many referendums have there been since the 1953 Constitution, and how many were about the EU?
16 referendums. Nine of them were about Denmark's relationship with the EU.
What is the elected assembly called in a municipality and in a region?
Municipality: municipal council (kommunalbestyrelse). Region: regional council (regionsråd).
Every fourth year (2017, 2021, 2025, etc.) – at the same time.
What is the idea behind local self-government?
That public tasks related to citizens' daily lives are handled as close to the citizens as possible.
What can you get help with at the municipality's citizen service (borgerservice)?
Answers to questions and practical matters, e.g. moving house, pensions, passports and driving licences.
Which tasks are the municipalities responsible for?
Nurseries, kindergartens, folkeskoler, help for the elderly and disabled, employment, integration, roads, waste, environment, leisure and cultural activities.
What is the chair of the municipal council called, and who elects them?
The mayor (borgmester; in Copenhagen: the Lord Mayor, overborgmester). Elected by the newly elected municipal council.
How many members does a municipal council have?
Typically 19–31 (down to 9 in the smallest municipalities, up to 55 in Copenhagen). Always an odd number.
Do the municipalities have the right to levy taxes?
Yes. The state also gives money to the municipalities.
What is the municipalities' interest organisation called?
Local Government Denmark (Kommunernes Landsforening, KL). Every year the government makes an economic agreement with KL.
How many regions are there in Denmark, and what are they called?
Five: the Capital Region, Zealand, Southern Denmark, Central Jutland and North Jutland.
What happens to the Capital Region and Region Zealand on 1 January 2027?
They merge into Region East Denmark (Region Østdanmark).
What are the regions responsible for, among other things?
Healthcare – they run the public hospitals.
Do the regions have the right to levy taxes?
No. They get their money directly from the state.
Who leads a region, and what is the regions' interest organisation called?
A regional council with a chair (elected by the regional council). Interest organisation: Danish Regions (Danske Regioner).
Which four elections are held in Denmark?
General (Folketing) elections, municipal elections, regional council elections and elections to the European Parliament.
What are the four political levels?
Local: the municipal council. Regional: the regional council. National: the Folketing. EU: the European Parliament.
When are referendums held?
On very specific matters, e.g. the voting age or when Denmark is to give up sovereignty (e.g. EU membership).
Who calls a general election, and how often must there be an election at least?
The prime minister. There must be an election at least every fourth year.
Which three requirements must you meet to vote in a general election?
Danish citizenship, being 18 or older and permanent residence in Denmark, the Faroe Islands or Greenland.
Is it compulsory to vote?
No. But about 85% normally vote in general elections.
What was voter turnout in the 2025 municipal and regional elections, and in the 2024 European Parliament election?
Municipal/regional 2025: 69%. European Parliament 2024: 58%.
Who may vote in municipal and regional elections?

Anyone 18 or older – Danish citizenship is not required. Also citizens of the EU, Norway and Iceland with permanent residence, and other foreigners who have lived permanently in Denmark for the four years before election day.
What does eligible for election (valgbar) mean?
That you can be elected. If you meet the conditions for voting, you are normally also eligible for election.
How are the Folketing's 179 members distributed?
175 elected in Denmark + 2 from the Faroe Islands + 2 from Greenland.
What share of those elected to the Folketing in 2026 are women?
49 percent.
What share of municipal council and regional council members are women?
Municipal councils: about 36%. Regional councils: about 50%.
How many members are there on each regional council?
41 (according to fact sheet 15; fact sheet 14 mentions 25–47).
How often are there elections to the European Parliament, and how many members does Denmark elect?
Every fifth year (2019, 2024, 2029 …). Denmark elects 15 members.
Who has the right to vote in the European Parliament election in Denmark?
Citizens of an EU country who are 18 or older.
What is a polling card (valgkort), and what must you do if you do not bring it?
Proof of your right to vote, with information about where and when to vote. Without a polling card you must bring ID.
What does a secret ballot mean?
That no one else may see what or whom you vote for.
How do you vote on the ballot paper?
Put a cross next to a party or a specific candidate. You can also cast a blank vote (no cross, often as a protest).
What is a postal / advance vote (brevstemme)?
Voting before election day – can be done anywhere in the country and at Danish embassies and missions abroad.
What is a political party?
An association that works for a particular political programme and puts up candidates for election.
What is an independent member (løsgænger)?
A member of the Folketing outside the parties (e.g. after leaving their party). The politician does not have to leave the Folketing.
Which parties got the most votes in the 2026 general election (top three)?
The Social Democrats, SF and Venstre.
How many Danes are members of a political party, and how are the parties financed?
About 106,000 members. Money from membership fees and from the state in proportion to the number of votes.
What is an interest organisation?
An association of people or companies with a common interest (e.g. a trade union, patients' association, farmers' organisation) that tries to influence politics.
What is a grassroots movement?
Less formally organised than an interest organisation – its strength comes from its participants' activity. Uses, for example, petitions and demonstrations.
Do you need permission to demonstrate?
No – but you must notify the police. The police can require the demonstration to move and can only ban it in very special circumstances.
What is the most common form of protest among grassroots movements?
Collecting signatures (petitions).
What three kinds of rights do citizens have?
Political rights, civil liberties and social rights.
What are political rights?
The right to vote and to stand as a candidate (Folketing, municipal council).
Which four civil liberties are mentioned?
Freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and freedom of association.
What are social rights?
The right to benefits and services if you need help – e.g. free medical care or financial support.
Which two duties are mentioned?
The duty to pay tax and conscription (military service).
What do you have to pay tax on?
Wages, many social benefits, SU, interest in the bank, gains from selling shares – and in some cases gifts.
Who is subject to conscription?
All men and women over 18 with Danish citizenship. Women have only been subject to conscription since 1 July 2025.
What is 'Forsvarets Dag' (Defence Day)?
Everyone is called in for tests and a health check. About half are declared fit. Then everyone draws a lottery number.
How long does military service last?
Normally 11 months in the Armed Forces and nine months in the Emergency Management Agency.
What can you do if you want to refuse military service in the Armed Forces or the Emergency Management Agency?
Apply for conscientious objector status and do your service e.g. in public institutions or relief organisations.
How many conscripts should there eventually be (decided in 2024)?
7,500 (in 2024 the number was 4,700).
When was freedom of religion confirmed in Denmark?
With the Constitution of 1849.
Can you change religion or have no religion?
Yes – you can freely change religion and can choose to have none at all.
According to the Constitution, which church is the Danish national church (folkekirken)?
The Evangelical Lutheran Church (Protestant).
When did Denmark break with the Catholic Church?
At the Reformation in 1536.
Are state and church separated in Denmark?
No. The state supports the national church financially – but the church has no political power.
What share are members of the national church (2026)?
About 70 percent.
What do many Danes use the national church for?
Baptism, confirmation, weddings and funerals – and quite a few go to church on Christmas Eve, 24 December.
What is church tax, and who pays it?
Paid by members of the national church for the upkeep of churches and churchyards. Non-members do not pay it.
How do you become a member of the national church?
Only by being baptised. You can freely leave.
Yes, if the person you are marrying is a member.
Who can be buried in a Danish churchyard?
Everyone – including non-members of the national church. The funeral can be religious or civil.
What tasks does the national church have besides church services?
Registering births, names and deaths.
What advantages does a recognised religious community get?
Members can (with limits) deduct contributions from their taxes, and the priest can be authorised to perform legally valid weddings.
How many recognised religious communities and congregations are there in Denmark?
435 – most of them are Christian.
How many countries are in the EU, and where is the headquarters?
27 countries. Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium.
How many EU countries have the euro, and does Denmark have it?
21 of 27. Denmark has kept the krone.
When did Denmark join the EU (then the EC)?
1973 – after a referendum.
What happened at the 1992 referendum?
The Danes voted no to the Maastricht Treaty. Denmark then negotiated the Danish opt-outs.
What are the Danish opt-outs (forbehold)?
Areas where Denmark does not take part in EU cooperation – including the euro and justice cooperation (police, criminal law, asylum, immigration, divorce, custody).
How can an opt-out be abolished?
After a new referendum in Denmark.
When was the defence opt-out abolished, and by what majority?
1 June 2022 – 67% voted yes, 33% no.
What is the European Council?
EU summits where heads of state and government (for Denmark the prime minister) adopt the EU's overall political guidelines.
Who takes part in the Council of Ministers?
Ministers from the member states' governments for the relevant area (e.g. environment ministers at environment meetings).
What is the European Commission, and how many commissioners does each country have?
Each EU country has one commissioner, who leads a policy area. Commissioners must work independently of their home country. Denmark's commissioner is Dan Jørgensen.
